newsitem.title: USA: U.S. July home starts seen up on rates, confidence.
newsitem.headline: U.S. July home starts seen up on rates, confidence.

text.p: Lower mortgage rates in July, along with improved consumer confidence and better weather, led economists to predict that U.S. homebuilding accelerated during the month to an annual rate of about 1.46 million units of housing starts from 1.45 million in June.
Forecasts gathered by Reuters for July activity ranged from 1.43 million to 1.49 million units on an annualized basis. The data are due on Tuesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
"Confidence is still high," noted Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.
Schaja forecast a rise to 1.47 million units.

The Northeast should bounce back from June levels, and the West will remain the strongest region, she said. But "in general, there is no region that is weak," Schaja said, adding that current levels likely represent a plateau.
One factor bolstering the housing industry was the so-called "wealth effect," in which an ebullient stock market fattened pocketbooks and increased consumer spending.
"Good investment returns and good earnings have bolstered demand for homes," said Astrid Adolfson, senior economist at MCM Moneywatch.
She predicted a 1.47 million-unit rate for July, and a peak of up to 1.50 million units during this interest rate cycle.

As long as rates remain low and there is demand for existing homes, builders will feel comfortable building new homes, she added. "They will build on spec without having a commitment for the new house" in this environment of low inflation and economic expansion, said Adolfson.
Sanwa Securities Chief Economist Michael Strauss agreed that there was more strength underlying the housing sector than might be revealed in the housing starts report.

He forecast a 1.48 million-unit July starts rate, with "the risk of an even stronger rebound than that." Housing starts were particularly buoyant in the Northeast and Midwest, where homebuilding was slowed in June by bad weather, he said.

Strauss said the only reason his July forecast was not stronger was that summer rains affected the Southeast. Nonetheless, housing "is one of the sectors that will provide stimulus to economic growth" in the third quarter, he said.
Even if housing starts and building permits were unchanged in July, the pace would reflect persistent solid demand, some analysts contended.

David Lereah, chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association of America, predicted housing starts would be flat. But "I still view that as pretty healthy," he said, adding that "we've have very healthy home sales numbers and inventories are still pretty low."
(( -- Lynn Adler, 212-859-1677, Aleksandrs Rozens, 212-859-1668, U.S. Mortgage Unit ))
